headline: Elon Musk, chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, unveiled a Tesla Roadster prototype that used rocket-style thrusters to leap off a ramp, clear five cars and land softly.
score_reason: Pool 7 lowered by 1: the demonstration was on Thursday 15 Oct, before the 16 Oct window, and the car is a prototype with no price or date.
importance_line: A long-promised car shown with a stunt interests Tesla reservation holders and shareholders, but it is a prototype with no price and no date, production is not due before 2028, and the thruster version is not approved for public roads.
summary: NBC News reports that Elon Musk, chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, showed a prototype of the second-generation Tesla Roadster on Thursday 15 Oct at a SpaceX test site in Texas, eight years after the car was first announced. Musk told the live audience that what they were about to see "was not AI or SI"; the car then slowly drove up a ramp shaped like half a roller coaster loop, sped off it, jumped over five other Teslas and landed softly in a cloud of condensation using cold-gas thrusters (jets of compressed gas). Tesla says the car did a second jump of 27 feet with a barrel roll, and that it went from 0 to 60 mph in 0.81 seconds, more than a second faster than the discontinued Model S Plaid; Tesla also says a fan-based suction system presses the car to the road and that its thrusters refill themselves. "Well, it worked!" Musk said, adding that "it's not necessarily a safety-optimized car" and that the Roadster might not be legal in every place. There is no price or release date, and Musk said production would not begin until 2028; Tesla plans three versions: Performance (road-ready, no thrusters), Thrust (race-ready, rear thrusters) and Rocket (invite-only, one seat, thrusters around the car, not approved for public roads), and reservations are open at a $50,000 deposit for the base model or $250,000 for the Thrust version. Musk first promised production in 2020, and he wants the car to reach about 383 mph and go 300 miles on one charge, less than half of what he first promised; these are Tesla's and Musk's claims, not tested figures.
notes: Event was Thursday 15 Oct (Texas), reported through 16 Oct; not carried in our 15 or 16 Oct pools, so it is new to our readers. The AP video page was blocked, so NBC News (its own report) is the source. machine_action true because the vehicle is shown launching, flipping and landing; NBC does not say whether it was driven or autonomous. Update: re-read the NBC News report in full on 17 Oct (the story was timed 16 Oct, 11:58 AM EDT, by Chris Perez, a News Associate at NBC News); a search for a second outlet with post-event facts found only pre-event coverage, so every detail rests on NBC News and on Tesla's claims as NBC reports them.
